claims.source: Corresponding orthologues could be also found in the I. ricinus transcriptome (Kotsyfakis et al., 2015) (GenBank Ac. Nos JAB79008, JAB84046 and JAB74800, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome database analysis and citation.

claims.claim: Two gene sequences related to ALAS and UROD in I. scapularis are clearly bacterial and most likely originate from bacterial contamination of the genomic DNA.
claims.source: Another two gene sequences related to 5-aminolevulinate synthase (ALAS, Vectorbase: ISCW020754) and uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD, Vectorbase: ISCW020804) are clearly bacterial and most likely originate from bacterial contamination of the genomic DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 1—figure supplement 5, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing clustering with bacterial sequences.

claims.claim: The bacterial ALAS and UROD genes do not contain introns and are flanked by other bacterial genes in the corresponding genomic regions.
claims.source: This conclusion was further corroborated by the fact that these genes do not contain introns and are flanked by other bacterial genes in the corresponding genomic regions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis.

claims.claim: The I. scapularis genome contains at least 225 genes encoding a variety of enzymes utilizing haem as a cofactor.
claims.source: Despite an incomplete haem biosynthetic pathway, the I. scapularis genome contains at least 225 genes encoding a variety of enzymes utilizing haem as a cofactor, such as respiratory chain cytochromes, catalase, and a large family of cytochrome P450 genes (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genomic database analysis.

claims.claim: Ticks must possess efficient mechanisms for the acquisition of exogenous haem, together with its intra- and extra-cellular transport to produce endogenous haemoproteins.
claims.source: Hence, ticks must possess efficient mechanisms for the acquisition of exogenous haem, together with its intra- and extra-cellular transport to produce endogenous haemoproteins.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of many haem-requiring enzymes despite incomplete haem biosynthesis.

claims.claim: Serum-fed I. ricinus ticks were capable of fully engorging and laying eggs similar to blood-fed ticks.
claims.source: Serum-fed ticks were capable of fully engorging and laying eggs similar to BF ticks (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by membrane feeding experiments and visual documentation.

claims.claim: Embryos in eggs laid by blood-fed females developed normally and gave rise to living larvae.
claims.source: Embryos in eggs laid by BF females developed normally as described for naturally-fed ticks (Santos et al., 2013) and gave rise to living larvae (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination and larval hatching observations, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: No embryonic development was observed in colourless eggs laid by serum-fed ticks.
claims.source: In contrast, no embryonic development was observed in colourless eggs laid by SF ticks, and accordingly, no larvae hatched from these eggs (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination of eggs.

claims.claim: No larvae hatched from eggs laid by serum-fed ticks.
claims.source: In contrast, no embryonic development was observed in colourless eggs laid by SF ticks, and accordingly, no larvae hatched from these eggs (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by larval hatching observations.

claims.claim: The presence of haemoglobin in the diet rescued the competence of embryos to develop normally.
claims.source: The presence of haemoglobin in the diet rescued the competence of embryos to develop normally and the number of larvae hatching from eggs laid by S+Hb-F ticks was comparable with BF ticks (Figure 2, bottom panels).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments with haemoglobin supplementation.

claims.claim: The number of larvae hatching from eggs laid by serum+haemoglobin-fed ticks was comparable with blood-fed ticks.
claims.source: The presence of haemoglobin in the diet rescued the competence of embryos to develop normally and the number of larvae hatching from eggs laid by S+Hb-F ticks was comparable with BF ticks (Figure 2, bottom panels).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by larval hatching observations in rescue experiments.

claims.claim: As little as one hundredth of the physiological concentration of haemoglobin in the diet is sufficient to maintain tick reproduction.
claims.source: The same rescue effect was observed for ticks fed on 1% and 0.1% haemoglobin (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) demonstrating that as little as one hundredth of the physiological concentration of haemoglobin in the diet is sufficient to maintain tick reproduction.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments with varying haemoglobin concentrations.

claims.claim: Eggs laid by blood-fed ticks contained 669 ± 45 pmol haem b/mg eggs.
claims.source: Eggs laid by BF ticks contained 669 ± 45 pmol haem b/mg eggs, whereas eggs laid by SF ticks contained virtually no haem (only 3 ± 1.6 pmol haem b/mg eggs).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC quantification of haem b in egg homogenates.

claims.claim: Eggs laid by serum-fed ticks contained only 3 ± 1.6 pmol haem b/mg eggs.
claims.source: Eggs laid by BF ticks contained 669 ± 45 pmol haem b/mg eggs, whereas eggs laid by SF ticks contained virtually no haem (only 3 ± 1.6 pmol haem b/mg eggs).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC quantification of haem b in egg homogenates.

claims.claim: Eggs from serum+10%haemoglobin-fed ticks contained 508 ± 79 pmol haem b/mg eggs.
claims.source: Eggs from the rescue experiment (S+Hb-F ticks) contained only slightly decreased haem levels (508 ± 79 pmol haem b/mg eggs) compared to BF ticks.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC quantification of haem b in egg homogenates.

claims.claim: Eggs from ticks fed with 1% haemoglobin contained 471 ± 17 pmol haem b/mg eggs.
claims.source: Eggs from ticks fed with sub-physiological levels (1% and 0.1%) of haemoglobin contained gradually decreasing haem levels (471 ± 17 and 229 ± 97 pmol haem b /mg eggs, respectively) (Figure 3A), but were still capable completing development and producing viable larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC quantification of haem b in egg homogenates.

claims.claim: Eggs from ticks fed with 0.1% haemoglobin contained 229 ± 97 pmol haem b/mg eggs.
claims.source: Eggs from ticks fed with sub-physiological levels (1% and 0.1%) of haemoglobin contained gradually decreasing haem levels (471 ± 17 and 229 ± 97 pmol haem b /mg eggs, respectively) (Figure 3A), but were still capable completing development and producing viable larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC quantification of haem b in egg homogenates.

claims.claim: Eggs with haem levels as low as 229 ± 97 pmol haem b/mg were still capable of completing development and producing viable larvae.
claims.source: Eggs from ticks fed with sub-physiological levels (1% and 0.1%) of haemoglobin contained gradually decreasing haem levels (471 ± 17 and 229 ± 97 pmol haem b /mg eggs, respectively) (Figure 3A), but were still capable completing development and producing viable larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC quantification and larval hatching observations.

claims.claim: No apparent differences were observed in vitellin levels in eggs from blood-fed and serum-fed ticks.
claims.source: In contrast to haem concentrations, no apparent differences were observed in vitellin levels in eggs from BF and SF ticks, as determined by quantitative Western blot analysis (Figure 3B) with specific antibodies raised against recombinant vitellin precursors, I. ricinus vitellogenin 1 (IrVg1) and vitellogenin 2 (IrVg2) (Supplementary file 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: Haemoglobin is replaceable by serum proteins as a nutritional source of amino acids needed for vitellogenesis.
claims.source: This result implies that haemoglobin is replaceable by serum proteins as a nutritional source of amino acids needed for vitellogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that vitellin levels are similar in eggs from blood-fed and serum-fed ticks.

claims.claim: The gene encoding haem oxygenase (HO) is missing in I. scapularis and other mites.
claims.source: Genome-wide analyses of I. scapularis and other mites revealed a common unique feature; the gene encoding haem oxygenase (HO) is missing, pointing to a lack of enzymatic degradation of haem in these Acari representatives (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genome-wide database analysis.

claims.claim: HO-mediated haem degradation results in the equimolar release of iron and biliverdin.
claims.source: HO-mediated haem degradation results in the equimolar release of iron and the linear tetrapyrrole product, biliverdin (Khan and Quigley, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research and established knowledge.

claims.claim: No trace of biliverdin IX or modified biliverdin was detected in I. ricinus gut homogenates.
claims.source: With the detection limit as low as 5 pmol, no trace of biliverdin IX or modified biliverdin showing a bilin-like light absorbance near 660nm was detected in I. ricinus gut homogenates.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC analysis with diode-array detection.

claims.claim: The presence of biglutamyl biliverdin IX in whole body extracts of the blood-fed mosquito, Aedes aegypti, was confirmed.
claims.source: In contrast to ticks, the presence of biglutamyl biliverdin IX in whole body extracts of the blood-fed mosquito, Aedes aegypti (Pereira et al., 2007), was confirmed by our method exploiting diode-array detection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC analysis with diode-array detection and citation.

claims.claim: IrFer1 levels were lower in guts of blood-fed compared to serum-fed ticks.
claims.source: IrFer1 levels were lower in guts and about equal in ovaries and salivary glands of BF compared to SF ticks (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2);
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: IrFer1 levels were about equal in ovaries and salivary glands of blood-fed compared to serum-fed ticks.
claims.source: IrFer1 levels were lower in guts and about equal in ovaries and salivary glands of BF compared to SF ticks (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2);
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: The average iron concentration in salivary glands and ovaries was independent of haemoglobin in the tick diet.
claims.source: Despite large variations within individual biological replicates, the average iron concentration in either tissue was independent of haemoglobin in the tick diet (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GF-AAS elemental analysis of iron.

claims.claim: The bioavailable iron in tick tissues originates from host serum components rather than from haemoglobin-derived haem.
claims.source: These results conclusively proved that the bioavailable iron in tick tissues originates from host serum components rather than from haemoglobin-derived haem.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from ferritin and elemental iron analysis showing no difference between blood-fed and serum-fed ticks.

claims.claim: Haem-containing haemosomes were not observed in the digest cells from serum-fed ticks.
claims.source: Accordingly, haem-containing haemosomes were not observed in the digest cells from SF ticks (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination of semi-thin sections.

claims.claim: Haemolymph collected from blood-fed ticks displayed a typical haem light absorbance maximum (Soret peak) around 400 nm.
claims.source: Haemolymph collected from BF ticks displayed a typical haem light absorbance maximum (Soret peak) around 400 nm, which is not present in haemolymph from SF ticks (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by spectrophotometric analysis of haemolymph.

claims.claim: The Soret peak is not present in haemolymph from serum-fed ticks.
claims.source: Haemolymph collected from BF ticks displayed a typical haem light absorbance maximum (Soret peak) around 400 nm, which is not present in haemolymph from SF ticks (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by spectrophotometric analysis of haemolymph.

claims.claim: Haem present in the haemolymph of fully engorged females originated only from the blood meal of adults, and not from previous feeding at the nymphal stage.
claims.source: This observation demonstrates that haem present in the haemolymph of fully engorged females originated only from the blood meal of adults, and not from previous feeding at the nymphal stage.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of Soret peak in serum-fed ticks.

claims.claim: Out of approximately 10 µmol of total haem acquired from a tick blood meal, only about 100 nmol (~1%) needs to be transported to the ovaries.
claims.source: We estimate that out of approximately 10 µmol of total haem acquired from a tick blood meal, only about 100 nmol (~1%) needs to be transported to the ovaries within a period of several days.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on calculations from experimental data.

claims.claim: In the cattle tick R. microplus, the most abundant haemolymph protein, named HeLp, was reported to bind haem in the haemocoel.
claims.source: In the cattle tick R. microplus, the most abundant haemolymph protein, named HeLp, was reported to bind haem in the haemocoel (Maya-Monteiro et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: The genome of I. scapularis contains at least five genes related to HeLp, annotated as carrier proteins (cp1‒5).
claims.source: The genome of I. scapularis contains at least five genes related to HeLp, annotated as carrier proteins (cp1‒5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genomic database analysis.

claims.claim: ir-cp3 mRNA was consistently up-regulated by blood-feeding.
claims.source: Expression profiling over I. ricinus developmental stages and tissues revealed that ir-cp3 mRNA was consistently up-regulated by blood-feeding and was predominantly expressed in the trachea-fat body complex and, to a lesser extent, in salivary glands and ovaries of adult females (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR expression analysis.

claims.claim: ir-cp3 was predominantly expressed in the trachea-fat body complex and, to a lesser extent, in salivary glands and ovaries of adult females.
claims.source: Expression profiling over I. ricinus developmental stages and tissues revealed that ir-cp3 mRNA was consistently up-regulated by blood-feeding and was predominantly expressed in the trachea-fat body complex and, to a lesser extent, in salivary glands and ovaries of adult females (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR expression analysis.

claims.claim: IrCP3 was most abundant in tick haemolymph.
claims.source: SDS PAGE and Western blot analysis revealed that IrCP3 was most abundant in tick haemolymph (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), where its levels were not affected by the presence or absence of haemoglobin in the tick diet (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE and Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: IrCP3 levels in haemolymph were not affected by the presence or absence of haemoglobin in the tick diet.
claims.source: SDS PAGE and Western blot analysis revealed that IrCP3 was most abundant in tick haemolymph (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), where its levels were not affected by the presence or absence of haemoglobin in the tick diet (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE and Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: Haem was associated with the ~ 300 kDa band of IrCP3 only in the haemolymph from blood-fed ticks.
claims.source: Native pore-limit PAGE, followed by detection of haem via its peroxidase activity with 3,3'-diminobenzidine (DAB), showed that haem was associated with the ~ 300 kDa band of IrCP3 only in the haemolymph from BF ticks (Figure 5C, DAB panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by native PAGE and DAB staining.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-cp3 resulted in the disappearance of the haem Soret peak in haemolymph.
claims.source: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-cp3 in I. ricinus females (ir-cp3 KD) resulted in the disappearance of the haem Soret peak (Figure 5D), a substantial (~80%) reduction in IrCP3 levels on SDS PAGE (Figure 5E), and the absence of IrCP3-associated DAB stained haem on the native gel (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments and spectrophotometric analysis.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-cp3 resulted in a substantial (~80%) reduction in IrCP3 levels.
claims.source: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-cp3 in I. ricinus females (ir-cp3 KD) resulted in the disappearance of the haem Soret peak (Figure 5D), a substantial (~80%) reduction in IrCP3 levels on SDS PAGE (Figure 5E), and the absence of IrCP3-associated DAB stained haem on the native gel (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments and SDS-PAGE analysis.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-cp3 resulted in the absence of IrCP3-associated DAB stained haem on the native gel.
claims.source: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-cp3 in I. ricinus females (ir-cp3 KD) resulted in the disappearance of the haem Soret peak (Figure 5D), a substantial (~80%) reduction in IrCP3 levels on SDS PAGE (Figure 5E), and the absence of IrCP3-associated DAB stained haem on the native gel (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments and native PAGE with DAB staining.

claims.claim: IrCP3 is the major haem-binding protein in I. ricinus haemolymph.
claims.source: These results collectively demonstrate that IrCP3 is the major haem-binding protein in I. ricinus haemolymph.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including native PAGE, DAB staining, and RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: Extracts from I. ricinus ovaries were colourless until the 3rd day after detachment (AD) from the host.
claims.source: Extracts from I. ricinus ovaries were colourless until the 3rd day after detachment (AD) from the host, and then the Soret peak absorbance gradually increased, indicating an increase in haem concentration up to 8 days AD (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by spectrophotometric analysis of ovary extracts.

claims.claim: The Soret peak absorbance in ovary extracts gradually increased, indicating an increase in haem concentration up to 8 days after detachment.
claims.source: Extracts from I. ricinus ovaries were colourless until the 3rd day after detachment (AD) from the host, and then the Soret peak absorbance gradually increased, indicating an increase in haem concentration up to 8 days AD (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by spectrophotometric analysis of ovary extracts.

claims.claim: Levels of IrVg1- and IrVg2-derived proteolytic products gradually increased after tick detachment.
claims.source: SDS PAGE and Western blot analysis of ovary homogenates revealed that levels of IrVg1- and IrVg2-derived proteolytic products gradually increased after tick detachment whereas IrCP3 remained constant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE and Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: IrCP3 levels in ovary homogenates remained constant after tick detachment.
claims.source: SDS PAGE and Western blot analysis of ovary homogenates revealed that levels of IrVg1- and IrVg2-derived proteolytic products gradually increased after tick detachment whereas IrCP3 remained constant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE and Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: The appearance of haem in tick ovaries was coincident with the occurrence of vitellins.
claims.source: Native pore-limit PAGE followed by DAB-based haem co-detection and Western blot analyses confirmed that the appearance of haem in tick ovaries was coincident with the occurrence of vitellins (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by native PAGE, DAB staining, and Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: I. ricinus vitellogenin genes (ir-vg1 and ir-vg2) are exclusively expressed in fully engorged females.
claims.source: I. ricinus vitellogenin genes (ir-vg1 and ir-vg2) are exclusively expressed in fully engorged females, predominantly in the gut, salivary glands and trachea-fat body complex, but not in the ovaries (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR expression analysis.

claims.claim: ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 are predominantly expressed in the gut, salivary glands and trachea-fat body complex, but not in the ovaries.
claims.source: I. ricinus vitellogenin genes (ir-vg1 and ir-vg2) are exclusively expressed in fully engorged females, predominantly in the gut, salivary glands and trachea-fat body complex, but not in the ovaries (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR expression analysis.

claims.claim: Vitellogenins must be transported from their site of synthesis to the ovaries.
claims.source: As vitellins are predominantly found in ovaries, their precursors (vitellogenins) must be transported from their site of synthesis to the ovaries.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that vitellins are found in ovaries but vitellogenin genes are not expressed there.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 resulted in a substantial decrease in mRNA levels of both vitellogenin genes in gut tissues.
claims.source: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 resulted in a substantial decrease in mRNA levels of both vitellogenin genes in gut tissues, and the same dual silencing effect was also observed at the protein level for IrVg1 and IrVg2 in tick ovary homogenates (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis after RNAi.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 resulted in dual silencing effect at the protein level for IrVg1 and IrVg2 in tick ovary homogenates.
claims.source: RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 resulted in a substantial decrease in mRNA levels of both vitellogenin genes in gut tissues, and the same dual silencing effect was also observed at the protein level for IrVg1 and IrVg2 in tick ovary homogenates (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis after RNAi.

claims.claim: Silencing of both ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 led to impaired development of tick ovaries.
claims.source: More importantly, silencing of both ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 led to impaired development of tick ovaries and concomitant reduction in haem content in this tissue (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by visual examination and HPLC analysis after RNAi.

claims.claim: Silencing of both ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 led to concomitant reduction in haem content in ovaries.
claims.source: More importantly, silencing of both ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 led to impaired development of tick ovaries and concomitant reduction in haem content in this tissue (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC analysis after RNAi.

claims.claim: Decreased levels of both IrVg1 and IrVg2 in ovary homogenates from ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 KD ticks were associated with the disappearance of DAB-stained haem.
claims.source: Additionally, native pore-limit PAGE followed by DAB-staining and Western blotting (Figure 6D) showed that decreased levels of both IrVg1 and IrVg2 in ovary homogenates from ir-vg1 and ir-vg2 KD ticks were associated with the disappearance of DAB-stained haem.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by native PAGE, DAB staining, and Western blot analysis after RNAi.

claims.claim: Vitellins are the major haem-binding proteins in I. ricinus ovaries.
claims.source: These results collectively show that vitellins are the major haem-binding proteins in I. ricinus ovaries and imply that the majority of haem is transported, along with vitellogenins, to the developing oocytes after tick detachment from the host.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including native PAGE, DAB staining, and RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: The majority of haem is transported, along with vitellogenins, to the developing oocytes after tick detachment from the host.
claims.source: These results collectively show that vitellins are the major haem-binding proteins in I. ricinus ovaries and imply that the majority of haem is transported, along with vitellogenins, to the developing oocytes after tick detachment from the host.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the coincident appearance of haem and vitellins in ovaries and RNAi results.

claims.claim: During evolution, ticks have lost most of the genes encoding haem biosynthesis as a consequence of their strict haematophagy.
claims.source: Therefore we hypothesise that during evolution, ticks have lost most of the genes encoding haem biosynthesis as a consequence of their strict haematophagy.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on comparative genomic analysis showing incomplete haem biosynthesis in blood-feeding ticks but complete pathway in non-blood-feeding mites.

claims.claim: PPOX, CPOX and FECH are not involved in haem biosynthesis in adult ticks.
claims.source: Two lines of evidence suggest that PPOX, CPOX and FECH are not involved in haem biosynthesis in adult ticks: (i) Earlier, it was reported for R. microplus that no radioactively labelled δ-aminolevulinic acid was incorporated into haem present in haemolymph and ovaries (Braz et al., 1999); (ii) Recently, we have shown that RNAi-mediated silencing of the terminal FECH did not exert any effect on tick engorgement, oviposition, and larval hatching (Hajdusek et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research and RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: Serum-fed triatomine Rhodnius prolixus were capable of laying eggs and giving rise to viable larvae.
claims.source: In contrast to ticks, serum-fed triatomine Rhodnius prolixus were capable of laying eggs and giving rise to viable larvae (Machado et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: Triatominae insects possess a complete haem biosynthetic pathway.
claims.source: As Triatominae insects possess a complete haem biosynthetic pathway (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000), they can apparently reproduce even in the absence of dietary haem.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a database/published resource.

claims.claim: In the majority of animals studied so far, haem degradation represents the main source of iron.
claims.source: In the majority of animals studied so far (including insect blood-feeders), haem degradation represents the main source of iron, and conversely, iron is mainly utilised for de novo haem biosynthesis (Zhou et al., 2007; Gozzelino and Soares, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Iron is mainly utilised for de novo haem biosynthesis in the majority of animals studied so far.
claims.source: In the majority of animals studied so far (including insect blood-feeders), haem degradation represents the main source of iron, and conversely, iron is mainly utilised for de novo haem biosynthesis (Zhou et al., 2007; Gozzelino and Soares, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: The HO gene was missing in the tick genome.
claims.source: We found that the HO gene was missing in the tick genome and correspondingly, the haem degradation product, biliverdin IX, could not be found in I. ricinus gut homogenates (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genomic database analysis and HPLC analysis.

claims.claim: The absence of the HO gene is a common feature in other mite genomes.
claims.source: We further noted that the absence of the HO gene is a common feature in other mite genomes (Figure 1B) and respective HO orthologues could not been found even in non-Acari genomes: the chelicerate genome of Stegodyphus mimosarum (Sanggaard et al., 2014) and the myriapode genome of Strigamia maritima (Chipman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genomic database analysis and citations.

claims.claim: HO orthologues could not be found in the chelicerate genome of Stegodyphus mimosarum and the myriapode genome of Strigamia maritima.
claims.source: We further noted that the absence of the HO gene is a common feature in other mite genomes (Figure 1B) and respective HO orthologues could not been found even in non-Acari genomes: the chelicerate genome of Stegodyphus mimosarum (Sanggaard et al., 2014) and the myriapode genome of Strigamia maritima (Chipman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genomic database analysis and citations.

claims.claim: The apparent absence of HO transcripts in two color-polymorphic spiders of the genus Theridion is in agreement with the notion that these animals do not produce bilin pigments as haem degradation products.
claims.source: The apparent absence of HO transcripts in two color-polymorphic spiders of the genus Theridion is in agreement with the notion that these animals do not produce bilin pigments as haem degradation products (Croucher et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: The HO gene is present in the genomes of Hexapoda and Crustacea.
claims.source: As HO gene is present in the genomes of Hexapoda (Adams et al., 2000; Holt et al., 2002) and Crustacea (Colbourne et al., 2011), we hypothesise that the loss of HO is an old ancestral trait of Chelicerata and Myriapoda that are phylogenetically supported as sister groups (Dunn et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published genome sequences.

claims.claim: The loss of HO is an old ancestral trait of Chelicerata and Myriapoda.
claims.source: As HO gene is present in the genomes of Hexapoda (Adams et al., 2000; Holt et al., 2002) and Crustacea (Colbourne et al., 2011), we hypothesise that the loss of HO is an old ancestral trait of Chelicerata and Myriapoda that are phylogenetically supported as sister groups (Dunn et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on comparative genomic analysis and phylogenetic relationships.

claims.claim: Chelicerata and Myriapoda are phylogenetically supported as sister groups.
claims.source: As HO gene is present in the genomes of Hexapoda (Adams et al., 2000; Holt et al., 2002) and Crustacea (Colbourne et al., 2011), we hypothesise that the loss of HO is an old ancestral trait of Chelicerata and Myriapoda that are phylogenetically supported as sister groups (Dunn et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published phylogenetic research.

claims.claim: Successful tick development and reproduction is strictly dependent on the availability of iron and maintenance of its systemic homeostasis.
claims.source: Earlier, we and others reported that successful tick development and reproduction is strictly dependent on the availability of iron and maintenance of its systemic homeostasis (Hajdusek et al., 2009; Galay et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Bioavailable iron originates from serum iron-containing proteins, most likely host transferrin.
claims.source: These results further support the conclusion that bioavailable iron does not originate from haemoglobin-derived haem, but rather from serum iron-containing proteins, most likely host transferrin (Hajdusek et al., 2009; Galay et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results and supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In the triatomine bug, R. prolixus, a 15-kDa haemolymphatic haem-binding protein (RHBP) was reported to transport haem to pericardial cells for detoxification and to growing oocytes for yolk granules.
claims.source: In the triatomine bug, R. prolixus, a 15-kDa haemolymphatic haem-binding protein (RHBP) was reported to transport haem to pericardial cells for detoxification and to growing oocytes for yolk granules as a source of haem for embryo development (Walter-Nuno et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: Haem transport and/or binding in ticks is mediated by HeLp/CPs and vitellins.

results.result: Ticks possess an incomplete haem biosynthetic pathway, retaining only the last three mitochondrial enzymes (CPOX, PPOX, FECH) while lacking the cytoplasmic enzymes. Genomic analysis revealed that genes annotated as ALAS and UROD in I. scapularis are bacterial contaminants.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C26, C33-C37 are well-supported by genomic database screening, phylogenetic analysis, and genomic sequence analysis showing the absence of most haem biosynthetic genes in ticks. The identification of bacterial contamination is corroborated by phylogenetic clustering, lack of introns, and flanking bacterial genes.

results.result: Ticks and all mites lack the gene encoding haem oxygenase (HO), which is also absent in other chelicerate and myriapod genomes but present in insects and crustaceans.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C27, C55, C101-C103 are supported by comprehensive genome-wide database analysis across multiple arthropod species and HPLC analysis confirming the absence of biliverdin IX (the HO product) in tick gut homogenates.

results.result: Ticks require dietary haemoglobin as an exogenous source of haem for successful reproduction. Serum-fed ticks can engorge and lay eggs but embryogenesis is aborted without haemoglobin.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C29, C40-C43 are strongly supported by membrane feeding experiments showing that serum-fed ticks produce colourless eggs with no embryonic development or larval hatching, demonstrating absolute haem auxotrophy for reproduction.

results.result: Supplementation of serum with haemoglobin fully rescues tick reproduction, with as little as 0.1% of physiological haemoglobin concentration being sufficient to maintain successful embryogenesis and larval hatching.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C44-C46 are supported by rescue experiments demonstrating dose-dependent restoration of embryonic development and larval hatching with haemoglobin supplementation, including at sub-physiological concentrations.

results.result: Haemoglobin can be completely substituted by serum proteins for the provision of amino acids in vitellogenesis, as vitellin levels in eggs are similar between blood-fed and serum-fed ticks.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C53, C54 are supported by quantitative Western blot analysis showing no significant differences in vitellin 1 and vitellin 2 levels between eggs from blood-fed and serum-fed ticks, demonstrating that haemoglobin is not required as a protein source.

results.result: Ticks do not acquire bioavailable iron from haemoglobin-derived haem. Iron in tick tissues originates from host serum components rather than haem, as evidenced by similar ferritin and elemental iron levels in tissues from blood-fed and serum-fed ticks.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C30, C59-C62, C120 are supported by quantitative Western blot analysis of ferritin levels and GF-AAS elemental iron analysis showing no significant differences between blood-fed and serum-fed ticks, conclusively demonstrating that haem is not a source of bioavailable iron.

results.result: Haem b content in tick eggs is directly dependent on dietary haemoglobin, ranging from 669 pmol/mg in blood-fed ticks to virtually zero (3 pmol/mg) in serum-fed ticks, with dose-dependent intermediate levels in rescue experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are supported by HPLC quantification showing clear dose-response relationship between dietary haemoglobin concentration and egg haem content, with even low haem levels (229 pmol/mg) sufficient for viable larval development.

results.result: No biliverdin IX or modified biliverdin was detected in I. ricinus gut homogenates, confirming the absence of haem degradation, while the positive control mosquito Aedes aegypti showed biglutamyl biliverdin IX.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by HPLC analysis with diode-array detection showing absence of biliverdin in ticks (detection limit 5 pmol) while confirming its presence in mosquitoes, providing functional evidence for lack of HO activity.

results.result: Acquired haem is distributed by haemolymph carrier proteins, as evidenced by the Soret peak at 400 nm in haemolymph from blood-fed but not serum-fed ticks. Only about 1% of total acquired haem needs to be transported to ovaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C64-C67 are supported by spectrophotometric analysis of haemolymph showing haem-specific absorbance only in blood-fed ticks and calculations based on experimental data estimating haem transport requirements.

results.result: IrCP3 is the major haem-binding protein in I. ricinus haemolymph during tick feeding. RNAi-mediated silencing of ir-cp3 resulted in disappearance of the haem Soret peak and ~80% reduction in IrCP3 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C78, C115 are strongly supported by multiple converging lines of evidence: qPCR expression analysis, SDS-PAGE and Western blot, native PAGE with DAB staining, and RNAi functional validation demonstrating IrCP3's essential role in haem binding.

results.result: Vitellins are the major haem-binding proteins in I. ricinus ovaries, with haem accumulation coincident with vitellin appearance after tick detachment. RNAi silencing of vitellogenin genes led to impaired ovary development and reduced haem content.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C79-C93, C117 are comprehensively supported by spectrophotometric analysis, native PAGE with DAB staining, Western blot analysis, qPCR expression profiling, and RNAi functional validation showing vitellins as essential haem-storage proteins for embryonic development.

results.result: Haem-containing haemosomes were not observed in digest cells from serum-fed ticks, consistent with the absence of dietary haemoglobin.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by microscopic examination of semi-thin sections showing haemosomes only in blood-fed ticks, providing morphological evidence consistent with the biochemical findings.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that ticks lost most genes encoding haem biosynthesis during evolution as a consequence of their strict haematophagy.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is explicitly stated as a hypothesis based on comparative genomic analysis. While the observation of incomplete haem biosynthesis in blood-feeding ticks versus complete pathways in non-blood-feeding mites is supported, the evolutionary causation remains speculative without phylogenetic reconstruction or experimental validation.

results.result: PPOX, CPOX, and FECH are not involved in haem biosynthesis in adult ticks, based on previous radiotracer studies and RNAi experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by citations to previous research showing no incorporation of radiolabeled δ-aminolevulinic acid into haem and RNAi silencing of FECH having no effect on tick reproduction, though these are prior studies rather than current work.

results.result: Despite incomplete haem biosynthesis, the I. scapularis genome contains at least 225 genes encoding haem-requiring enzymes, necessitating efficient mechanisms for exogenous haem acquisition and transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by genomic database analysis identifying haem-requiring enzymes. The inference about necessary transport mechanisms (C39) is logical given the presence of these enzymes despite haem auxotrophy.

results.result: Complete haem biosynthetic pathways are present in insects and non-blood-feeding mites (T. urticae and M. occidentalis), while substantially reduced in the blood-feeding tick I. scapularis.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by genomic analysis and citations to published genome sequences, providing comparative context for understanding tick haem auxotrophy.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that loss of HO is an old ancestral trait of Chelicerata and Myriapoda, which are phylogenetically supported as sister groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 present a hypothesis about HO loss being ancestral to Chelicerata and Myriapoda. While C107 (sister group relationship) is supported by citation, C106 remains speculative without formal ancestral state reconstruction or broader taxonomic sampling.

results.result: Bioavailable iron originates from serum iron-containing proteins, most likely host transferrin, rather than from haemoglobin-derived haem.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 is supported by the experimental results showing iron independence from haemoglobin and citations to previous research on transferrin uptake in ticks, though direct identification of transferrin as the source requires additional experiments.

results.result: Haem is mainly transported to developing ovaries during the off-host digestive phase, though the relative contributions of IrCP3 versus vitellogenins remain to be investigated.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by spectrophotometric analysis showing haem accumulation in ovaries after detachment. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about transport mechanisms is appropriate given current data limitations.

results.result: Ticks lack functional haem biosynthesis and recycle dietary haem, representing a major departure from canonical haem and iron homeostasis in other eukaryotic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C118, C119, C121 are summary conclusions well-supported by the collective experimental evidence demonstrating haem auxotrophy, absence of haem degradation, and separation of haem and iron metabolism.

results.result: Background claims about haem biology, other haem auxotrophs, haem toxicity, tick physiology, and haem transport in other organisms, all supported by citations to published literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C25, C28, C56, C68, C97-C100, C104-C105, C108, C110-C114, C122 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide context but are not novel findings of this study.
